title: Self-service isn’t the finish line. It’s where the real work begins.
summary: The self-service gap is more than finding information. Learn how benefits self-service can help employees take action.
body_markdown:
### Share


When employees have a question, need to understand a benefit, or want to figure out what to do next, they increasingly start online. Self-service is not something people need to be convinced to use, because it is already part of how they navigate service.


Gartner found that[73% of customers use self-service at some point in their service journey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-08-19-gartner-survey-finds-only-14-percent-of-customer-service-issues-are-fully-resolved-in-self-service) . The demand for self-service is there.


The problem is what happens next.


## Using self-service and resolving an issue are not the same thing


A person can find an answer without finding a resolution.


That distinction is easy to miss when self-service is measured by searches, page views, chatbot interactions or visits. Those metrics tell us someone engaged with information. They do not necessarily tell us whether that person accomplished what they came to do.


The gap is significant. Gartner found that only[14% of customer service and support issues are fully resolved through self-service](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-08-19-gartner-survey-finds-only-14-percent-of-customer-service-issues-are-fully-resolved-in-self-service) . Even when customers describe an issue as “very simple,” only 36% resolve it fully through self-service.


In other words, self-service often answers the question without finishing the job. That changes how we should think about the value of self-service. The goal is not simply to make information available. The goal is to help someone reach an outcome.


## The failure isn’t access. It’s understanding.


When self-service falls short, the instinct can be to assume there is not enough information. But the data points somewhere else.


Among customers who started their journey in self-service,[45% said the company did not understand what they were trying to do](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-08-19-gartner-survey-finds-only-14-percent-of-customer-service-issues-are-fully-resolved-in-self-service) . And the most common reason for self-service failure was not finding content relevant to the issue, cited in 43% of cases.


The information may exist. The problem is that the person cannot connect that information to their situation.


Someone trying to understand a deductible, find the right place to submit a claim or determine whether a particular service is covered does not necessarily need more information. They need information that recognizes what they are trying to accomplish and helps them take the next step.


That is the self-service gap: the distance between finding information and knowing what to do with it.


## In benefits, the cost of that gap is higher


For benefits, this distinction matters even more because information is only valuable when it changes behavior.


Members who understand their benefits are substantially more likely to use them,[roughly three times as likely](https://www.payrollintegrations.com/insights/employee-benefits-trends-for-meeting-the-needs-of-a-multigenerational-workforce) , according to benefits research. At the same time,[roughly 52% of people](https://www.benefitnews.com/news/metlife-shares-strategies-for-a-successful-2025-open-enrollment) still do not fully understand the benefits available to them.


Benefits are not simply information people consume. They are resources people are expected to act on: choosing coverage, finding care, using an account, submitting a claim, understanding what is covered or making a decision at an important moment in their lives.


When understanding is low, utilization can be low too.


And when a self-service experience provides an explanation without helping someone move forward, the result is not merely a frustrating digital interaction. It can mean a member does not use a benefit they have access to, delays an action they need to take or gives up and looks elsewhere for help.


The value and information about the benefit is there, but the outcome never happens.


## The real measure of self-service is action


This is why the conversation about self-service needs to move beyond access.


For years, the ambition has been straightforward: make information easier to find, make answers easier to access and give people more ways to help themselves. Those are worthwhile goals. But they stop short of the outcome that actually matters.


An employee wants to know whether something is covered. They want to find the right provider, understand what they owe, and use the benefit they have.


The question is not whether people will use self-service.


The question is whether self-service can understand what they are trying to accomplish and help them take action.
